However, we said that if it was necessary for the witness to leave, we had no cross-examination and, instead, we just wanted to read out this portion of the judgement. So that was the only reason why we wanted to do that. If you so wish, he may read it out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will start by reading. This is case P1437, page 82, in e-court, the last paragraph, and the first paragraph on the next page, as well as page 111 in e-court, in the English version. The relevant portion reads as follows: "The accused --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I saw Ms. Hasan on her feet and this is -- the Chamber would not accept to have this instead of a cross-examination. The words of Mr. Tolimir could be misunderstood. The witness yesterday was not under time pressure. He should have or could have come back to the courtroom today. This was not the question. You didn't have any cross-examination, Mr. Tolimir, and there is no replacement of cross-examination by reading a text. But despite of that, despite of that, Mr. Gajic should read the text now, and Ms. Hasan is no longer on her feet. Please continue, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This being an official document, we would appreciate having it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the relevant portion the document reads as follows: "The accused Branislav Medic, in his Defence --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The interpreters asked for the document on the screen. I think that would be helpful for the interpreters. You said this is P1437, page 82, in e-court. In that case, we need both versions. We have now only the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version, that's paragraph -- second paragraph on this page. Yes, now we have the right versions in both languages. In the Serbian language it is in the last paragraph of this page. With the Chamber's permission, I would like to read out this portion: "The accused Branislav Medic said in his defence that on the critical date he had received an order to transport the prisoners to the place of execution from Republika Srpska army officers whom he had never seen before and never saw again. Such a defence by the accused Branislav Medic was obviously aimed at easing the position of the accused Slobodan Medic and the same is contradictory to the -- in contradiction to the defence of the accused Petrasevic, Pera, and Aleksandar Medic as well as the testimony of Stojkovic Slobodan, whose words the Court believed and on the basis of which the Court established that it was Slobodan Medic himself who was the one who had sent them on assignment on the relevant morning and issued a concrete order to Petrasevic to execute those prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This was part of this document read into the record which itself is already in evidence as we have received the judgement yesterday as an exhibit. Mr. Gajic, you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. And I will be very brief. Because of the nature of the -- of this paragraph we did not wish to read it out in the witness's presence. That's the first thing I meant to say. And secondly, I just wanted -- we just wanted to read it out in order to underline the position of this Defence on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means the Defence in this case. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and this was clearly the kind of argument that I was mentioning, and if I could have 30 seconds to underline the Prosecution's position on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the Prosecution's position, Mr. President, that it wasn't just the Skorpion group that we saw that decided on their own to kill these six men. It is clearly the result of orders from high above, and I would point out for you that these men came all the way across -- the Srebrenica victims that you've seen, it's been already proven, came all the way across Bosnia from Srebrenica, were distributed to these people. There was no way this was just one unit doing this, that it came on orders from a much higher authority, and you will see the evidence related to that and I believe you will conclude that it came from a higher authority, which happens to be consistent with this particular Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, that was the position of the OTP and you were not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. And as I would imagine, we must view the same thing from what Mr. Gajic did; and I referred to some evidence and he's referred to some evidence, and I hope that you find that helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this concludes this matter. I would like to turn to another matter. On Monday, the 29th of November, this Monday, the parties made submissions regarding the cross-examination of the witness Tomasz Blaszczyk. The Chamber has considered carefully the submissions of the parties and the Chamber now wishes to request the accused to clarify his request. Mr. Tolimir, there are some unclear issues. The first one is we understood that you requested more time. Could you tell us for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have to review all those diaries in order to see whether what Mr. Blaszczyk was telling us about these diaries is credible or not. Those diaries were found so much time after the war. Some people raised an issue of their authenticity, and that's why we need time to form our own opinion. I told you clearly when I spoke about that, when Mr. Blaszczyk testified, that General Tolimir accepted everything that his commander either wrote or said about him during the war but I don't know whether I have anything to add to that or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. I take it that you are referring your request just to the diaries tendered through the witness Tomasz Blaszczyk on the hearing and during the examination-in-chief on Monday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. That's correct. That's what I meant. The material is voluminous and I never had an opportunity to read those materials before, so I would like to see whether anything was added to them after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey? You are on your feet and could you please remind us, when were these diaries of Mr. Mladic were disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There is two sets of disclosure. Two different searches of the Mladic residence. One was a few years ago and -- where the diary from 1995, the most relevant period for this case, was retrieved. It's the one you may recall that was on the video that you can see him writing in. This has been around for a long time. Ms. Stewart is going to tell me exactly when. But it was provided to the Defence early on in this case, and they've had several months, if not years, to review it. Having said that, I don't feel the need to rush the general on these points, but the most relevant in many respects, the 1995 diary, was provided -- and I will give you the date because I see she's about to write it down. There is the -- 20th April 2009. So, yes, years ago. And the second group, when the Serb authorities went back into the same house and found -- as you heard, found this secreted behind a wall or something, was provided on the 8th of April 2010. This is a more recent group. It is -- there is important material in there. There is actually some material from 1995 in that second group as well. So I don't mean to rush the general with this, but when he says, "I never have had a chance to review it," he needs to be reminded that he's had it for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one thing that I would like to say, something has not been recorded, as Mr. Tolimir told me. This was not done not because we didn't have enough time; the disclosures followed the schedule explained to us by Mr. McCloskey. However, the materials were not on the 65 ter list before the trial, and in the course of the trial, most of our attention is dedicated to the materials that the OTP intends to use during trial. That's number 1. Secondly, the notebooks cover a long period, even the period that is not covered by the indictment. Here, we have about 20 binders of material that have been admitted into evidence. Thousands of pages. It's a very tall order to review all those pages, a task which takes time. If we are talking about relevance, Mr. Tolimir stated here that, yes, we reviewed the key dates in 1995. We have reviewed all those. However, everything that has been seized has been entered into evidence. We have not had an occasion to see all that, and that was due to the lack of time. We couldn't believe that the OTP would ever tender all of that into evidence. That's the main reason why we are asking for additional time before we are able to cross-examine Mr. Blaszczyk. If the Prosecution has requested admission only of the materials covering the year 1995, we would have been ready to start our cross-examination the moment the Prosecutor finished his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, please clarify something. You triggered again some confusion. Mr. Tolimir was referring to the diaries, I think 29 diaries, of Mr. Mladic. Now you say here we have about 20 binders of the material that have been admitted into evidence, thousands of pages. What is that about? We need some information about that. I'm really confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I may not have been clear enough. We are talking about materials that have been admitted through Witness Blaszczyk. We are talking about a volume of 20 binders. I'm not sure about the exact number of items of evidence. However, the notebooks plus the material introduced through Mr. Blaszczyk is what we have received, we as a Defence, in the form of 20 binders of printed material, and you will agree with us that that's a lot, a very voluminous read. I'm not sure about the number of pages. Please don't hold me to the number of pages that I mentioned. If necessary, we will be able to provide you with the precise figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, in the list before me from the search of the 22nd of February 2010, I only see "Description of material: Handwritten notebook, handwritten notebook," and so on. I think quite a lot of them. Only the last one is -- has a title, "Original spiral-bound notebook with handwritten entries of Ratko Mladic." Are you referring solely to these materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those, plus the materials, and if I remember well, there was a table used by the Prosecution in order to establish the authenticity of the materials, i.e. the notebooks, which were being admitted. Again, another quite voluminous read, a lot of pages that have to be reviewed very carefully. All that constitutes about 20 binders. Our associates in this case have printed the relevant portions, the relevant material, and we have ended up with a total of 20 binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are these copies of the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, copies of the notebooks, plus some other materials. Notebooks account for some 90 per cent of the total read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, Mr. Tolimir told us that he was only referring to, I think, 29 notebooks. And you always say "additional material."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to make myself very clear, let's ignore the additional material. However, the notebooks themselves are voluminous and they cover a period from 1991 through 1995 or 1996. Just to leaf through all that material would take a lot of time. All that has been admitted into evidence already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To clarify and to request that they get their facts straight when they make these kind of arguments, because I'm really getting tired of it, and trying to build 65 ter into something it is not, which is some sort of Rule for the admissibility of evidence. The key 1995 Mladic diary that he's had for years has had 65 ter number 5490 since the beginning and they've had it from the beginning. So enough of that nonsense. The same with two other of the diaries. Now, I will agree with him the other, newer diaries are voluminous and the materials in support of them are voluminous and we don't have a problem with him and the general getting time to take a look at those materials. There is no problem there. But this illustrates the problem of having no legal representation. They keep taking this "no position." They didn't object to the Mladic diaries. They took no position. Now they are clearly taking an objection position. Any lawyer knows that this position of no position constantly used over and over again is no strategy. It's not lawyering. It's inappropriate, it's confusing, and it will lead to this kind of dialogue. So I would please, if they would consider this position of no position, it takes us nowhere except to a proper lawyer, because this is not proper lawyering, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that this was inappropriate. This reaction was inappropriate. And we are not in a position to take a position on something that we have not had an occasion to review completely. At the moment when we do review all those things, we will have a position, we will take a position. I don't see a problem even in not taking a position on something. This is the Prosecution case, is it not? And the Prosecutor is the one that has to prove things beyond reasonable doubt. The Prosecutor is the one who, in this stage, holds the primary responsibility of admitting things into evidence. And if the Defence does not take a position but leaves it to the Chamber to do that, isn't that a legitimate position? We do not have to have a position on every single thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we should stop this discussion. We just wanted to know what is the position in respect to the material. I take it you are referring to those materials tendered and admitted through the evidence of Mr. Blaszczyk and that you need more time to examine -- to cross-examine Mr. Blaszczyk on this material. If that is the case, I think we have reached an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes. I believe that we have indeed reached an agreement. There is no doubt about that, we need some more time. I apologise, I forgot to respond to something else that Mr. McCloskey raised. Not all the diaries were on 65 ter list. We didn't take a position, we didn't voice an objection either. Everything was admitted. We didn't have any objection, so I don't see a -- any reason for any heightened emotions in the courtroom. I believe that our cooperation regarding procedural issues has been good. Defence had a liberal position on the expansion of the 65 ter list, and in this specific situation we are not asking for anything else but some additional time. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I repeat: We should stop this discussion. We -- the Chamber invites the Defence to provide us with a specific request during our hearing on Monday what you mean by "additional time," what amount of time do you need for preparation of the cross-examination of Mr. Blaszczyk, and then the Prosecution will be in the position to respond to that and the Chamber will make a finding. I hope this request to the Defence is clear. Thank you very much. We are at the end of today's hearing. We adjourn and resume on Monday, in the afternoon, 2.15, in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
